findings.headline: DSG deficit of £7.331m to be 90% written off by High Needs Stability Grant, leaving council to fund 10%
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant Reserve held a deficit of £7.331m as at 31 March 2026. The Department for Education's High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of this accrued deficit, leaving the Council responsible for managing and funding the remaining 10% (approximately £733k). Future deficits accrued in 2026/27 onwards may be covered by future HNSG payments, but this is not yet confirmed by DfE as their review of High Needs funding continues.
findings.matters: Partial bailout masks underlying structural high-needs funding gap; future DSG deficits uncertain and could resume accumulating if HNSG support is not confirmed
findings.figures: £7,331k DSG deficit at 31 March 2026; 90% written off by HNSG; Council responsible for £733k; future HNSG payments not yet confirmed
findings.quote: This one-off Grant will write-off 90% of the accrued DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026, with the Council responsible for managing and funding the remaining 10%. Deficits accrued in 2026/27 and beyond may be covered by future HNSG payments, but this is yet to be confirmed by the DfE

findings.headline: Asset Disposal Plan is critical to financial position, required to cover £6.663m Growth & Prosperity and £4.966m Flexible Use of Capital Receipts targets
findings.detail: Forecast Earmarked Revenue Reserves of £21.34m assume that in-year Growth & Prosperity deficit (£6.663m) and Flexible Use of Capital Receipts target (£4.966m) are covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. An Asset Disposal working group has been established, meeting monthly, and is developing a contingency plan to mitigate delivery risk. Total of £11.6m in required disposals underpins the current financial forecast.
findings.matters: Primary mechanism for balancing the position depends on achieving significant asset sales; failure to deliver disposals would immediately create £11.6m financing gap
findings.figures: £6,663k G&P overspend dependent on Asset Disposal; £4,966k Flexible Use of Capital Receipts dependent on Asset Disposal; total £11.629m
findings.quote: This figure also assumes the in-year Growth & Prosperity (£6.663m) and the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts target (£4.966m) are covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. An Asset Disposal working group has been set up and is meeting monthly to progress these disposals

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate 3rd lowest in England at 26% at month 3, reflecting deprivation, with recovery pressures mounting
findings.detail: Being the most deprived local authority in England, Council Tax collection is identified as a challenge. The 2025/26 collection rate dipped from 4th lowest to 3rd lowest in England. At end month 3, £21.8m collected at 26% collection rate. Cumulative collection on arrears (2020/21 to 2025/26) at 91.4%. The Council Tax Reduction Scheme collection is under 'similar pressure' due to accumulated arrears and cost of living impact on household income.
findings.matters: Weak collection rates on main revenue source, with accumulated arrears and cost-of-living pressures suggesting continued headwinds to income recovery
findings.figures: 26.0% collection rate at month 3; 3rd lowest in England for 2025/26; cumulative arrears collection rate 91.4%; CTRS collection rate 20.8%
findings.quote: Being the most deprived local authority in England per the Office for National Statistics, collection of Council Tax is a challenge and 2025/26 saw the collection rate dip from 4th lowest in England to 3rd lowest

findings.headline: Council borrowing nearly doubled from £250m (2017/18) to £587m (2025/26) with 50:50 split between long and short-term at rates exceeding 6%
findings.detail: Council borrowing has grown from less than £250m at end 2017/18 to £587m at end 2025/26, forecast to £605m. The borrowing profile changed to 50:50 long-term and short-term split as at 2025/26, after shorter 'long-term' borrowing was taken in 2025/26. Long-term PWLB rates currently exceed 6% despite base rate at 3.75%. Month 3 2026/27 shows long-term borrowing increased by £28.4m.
findings.matters: Doubling of borrowing stock combined with elevated long-term rates and shift to shorter-term debt increases refinancing and interest rate risk exposure
findings.figures: £587m at 2025/26; forecast £605m for 2026/27; long-term rates >6%; short-term borrowing increased £28.4m in first 3 months
findings.quote: Council borrowing has doubled from less than £250m at the end of 2017/18 to £587m at the end of 2025/26. The profile of this borrowing has also changed to a 50:50 split of long-term and short-term borrowing as at 2025/26

findings.headline: Strategic Leisure Assets (Tower and Winter Gardens) forecast £1.721m overspend with cumulative deficit expected to reach £12.474m
findings.detail: Strategic Leisure Assets is forecasting a £1.721m pressure in 2026/27. Cumulative deficit expected to reach £12.474m by 31 March 2027. The council notes that under the original 2011 Executive decision, any over/underspend is transferred to an Earmarked Reserve. A new leisure assets medium-term financial plan is being worked up following management change (creation of Blackpool Tourism Limited). The previous plan expected to break-even cumulatively by 2034/35.
findings.matters: Long-term cultural/tourism investment with significant accumulated deficit and uncertain breakeven timeline; dependent on Blackpool Tourism Limited's commercial performance
findings.figures: £1,721k forecast pressure; £12,474k cumulative deficit forecast at 31 March 2027; previous MTFP expected breakeven by 2034/35
findings.quote: Strategic Leisure Assets, which largely relates to the investment in key historic and economic assets of Blackpool Tower and the Winter Gardens, forecast a pressure of £1,721k... cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2027 will be £12,474k

findings.headline: Growth and Prosperity schemes creating £8.049m in-year pressure with cumulative deficit forecast at £10.273m
findings.detail: Growth and Prosperity schemes are forecasting an £8.049m pressure (£6.663m from schemes, £1.386m from Enterprise Zone). Cumulative deficit at 31 March 2027 expected to be £10.273m for Growth & Prosperity and £2.166m for Enterprise Zone. The council notes this is treated as 'nil' variance as it assumes the in-year deficit will be covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. These investments are described as having 'long term financial payback' but create 'short to medium term challenge'.
findings.matters: Major speculative investment in jobs and economic regeneration is accumulating deficits dependent on asset sales; delivery risk on disposal plan threatens consolidated position
findings.figures: £8,049k pressure; £10,273k cumulative deficit G&P; £2,166k cumulative deficit Enterprise Zone
findings.quote: The service is forecasting a £8,049k pressure which is made up of £6,663k from Growth & Prosperity schemes and £1,386k from the Enterprise Zone... This investment in jobs and the economy, in projects such as the Civil Service Hub and Enterprise Zone infrastructure, presents a short to medium term challenge, with long term financial payback

findings.headline: Earmarked Revenue Reserves forecast to decline from £27.2m to £21.3m in-year, then to £14.7m by March 2028
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, Earmarked Revenue Reserves stood at £27.185m. The forecast shows decline to £21.34m by 31 March 2027 and further to £14.7m by 31 March 2028. Key drawdowns include £6.663m from Growth and Prosperity reserve, £1.721m from Strategic Leisure Assets, and £1.386m from Enterprise Zone, assuming Asset Disposal Plan delivers as expected.
findings.matters: Multi-year reserve depletion trajectory shows the council is funding current operations partly from reserves and special initiatives; unsustainable without new revenue sources
findings.figures: £27.185m at 1 April 2026; forecast £21.34m at 31 March 2027; forecast £14.7m at 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Earmarked Revenue Reserves (ERR) as at 31 March 2026 are £27.185m, however, these are forecast to reduce to £21.340m by 31 March 2027

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements forecast £4.2m overspend driven by residential placements at 78 against capacity
findings.detail: Residential placements are at 78 as at 30 June 2026, forecast to reduce to 64 by 31 March 2027. The council reports 531 children in care (188 per 10,000 population 0-17), higher than statistical neighbours will be post-Local Government Reforms. Residential care unit costs and volumes are the two largest drivers of the budget pressure. The council is using Care Cubed benchmarking tool to negotiate with providers and working to step children into lower-cost foster care and semi-independent settings.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressure on a statutory service with no capacity to underspend; residential placement rates above national average reflect service complexity and cost exposure
findings.figures: £4,203k forecast overspend; 78 residential placements (forecast 64); 531 children in care; £3,384k of the overspend from placements
findings.quote: Children's Social Care Placements are forecasting an overspend of £3,384k, mainly due to new-to-care placements being higher than those exiting care and the additional support required following the breakdown of high-cost placements

findings.headline: Working balances forecast to fall to £2.08m against a £7.8m target, leaving minimal headroom
findings.detail: The Council set a target of £7.8m working balances by 31 March 2027 but is forecasting only £2.08m after accounting for a £6.9m budgeted transfer at the start of the year. This represents a sharp decline from historic levels and leaves the Council with very limited buffer for volatility or unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Working balance depletion below prudent levels signals increased financial fragility and restricted capacity to absorb future shocks, a key indicator of lending risk
findings.figures: £2,080k forecast at end 2026/27 vs £7.8m target; working balances shown declining from peaks over £6m in prior years
findings.quote: Working balances are expected to show a balance of £2,080k by the end of 2026/27 after taking account of the budgeted transfer of £6,900k to working balances at the start of the year

findings.headline: COVID recovery loan repayment was extended from 5 to 10 years in February 2025
findings.detail: The Shareholder Committee extended the original 5-year repayment term for COVID-related loans to up to 10 years, with individual companies' periods to be determined case-by-case. This extension indicates the companies could not meet the original repayment schedule.
findings.matters: Extending repayment terms for loss-making subsidiaries shows the council is accommodating ongoing financial stress rather than enforcing commercial discipline. This signals a pattern of forbearance that may continue to require council support.
findings.figures: Repayment period extended from 5 to 10 years
findings.quote: On 4 February 2025, Shareholder Committee authorised an extended repayment period of up to 10 years for COVID recovery loans to follow the initial 5-year term with any repayment period to be determined on a case-by-case basis.

findings.headline: Council has loaned £61.47m to subsidiaries forecasting losses
findings.detail: The council has provided £57.99m in capital expenditure loans and £3.48m in cash flow loans to wholly-owned companies that are forecasting a consolidated loss of £2.343m for 2026/27. This large loan portfolio supports loss-making entities with no clear path to profitability.
findings.matters: Loans to loss-making subsidiaries represent contingent liability exposure. If WOC performance deteriorates, the council may face impairment charges, need to support further funding needs, or eventually absorb losses, affecting its financial position.
findings.figures: Capex loans £57.99m, cash flow loans £3.48m, total £61.47m; WOC forecast loss £2,343k
findings.quote: The Council's exposure to principal and capitalised interest in respect of such WOC capex loans is currently £57.99m.

findings.headline: Wholly-owned companies carry accumulated losses of £18.6m
findings.detail: The aggregated balance sheet shows retained losses of £18.566m, representing accumulated deficits over multiple years. Combined with the 2026/27 forecast loss of £2.343m, the companies have not achieved financial recovery despite COVID support, and asset value has deteriorated.
findings.matters: Accumulated losses represent eroded asset value in council-owned subsidiaries. A lender assessing council creditworthiness needs to evaluate whether the council will continue subsidizing these companies or if they represent an ongoing contingent liability.
findings.figures: Retained losses (18,566)k; 2026/27 forecast loss 2,343k
findings.quote: Profit & loss retained  (18,566)

findings.headline: Council is positioning debt portfolio to hedge interest rate risk, maintaining 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Panel has deliberately maintained a 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing for 2026/27 to offset economic uncertainty. This is operationalised through active short-term money market management, with £204m received and £526m paid out in Q1 alone, against a full-year budget of £247m for payments.
findings.matters: This shows how the council is managing interest rate risk in an uncertain environment. The deliberate portfolio positioning, combined with active short-term operations, indicates thoughtful treasury stewardship. It also flags that the council expects continued economic uncertainty to persist through the year.
findings.figures: 50:50 long-term/short-term split; £204m money market receipts and £526m payments in Q1 against £247m full-year payment budget
findings.quote: The Treasury Management Panel retain the 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing for 2026/27 to offset the effect of economic uncertainty.

findings.headline: Loan receipts exceeded budget by £292m in the first quarter, with total annual variance of £397m
findings.detail: The council received £315m in loans in Q1 (Apr-Jun) compared to a budgeted £23m for the quarter—nearly 14 times the planned amount. Against a full-year budget of only £28m, the Q1 actual alone represents a £292m variance. The Jul-Mar forecast shows another £110m. The commentary explicitly attributes this to the need to finance planned and approved capital expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council's actual borrowing trajectory versus the plan. A variance of nearly £400m on a £28m budget signals either material underestimation of capital needs or acceleration of planned schemes. This reshapes the debt position for the year.
findings.figures: £315m actual (Q1) vs £23m budget; £28m full-year budget vs £397m annual variance
findings.quote: 28 23 315 110 Receipt of Loans 292 105 397

findings.headline: Council took £28.4m in short-term borrowing at lower interest rates to fund capital expenditure in Q1.
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing increased by £28.4m during the first quarter explicitly to take advantage of lower interest rates for capital funding. The council's short-term borrowing position stands at £322m at end of June, with forecasts showing this will reduce to £275m by year-end as capital spending accelerates and longer-term refinancing occurs.
findings.matters: Lenders track a council's debt trajectory and refinancing strategy; rate-opportunistic borrowing indicates active treasury management, but the short-term nature and dependence on capex timing requires ongoing monitoring of how debt is refinanced.
findings.figures: £28.4m short-term borrowing increase; short-term borrowing £322m at M3 (30 June 26), forecast £275m by 31 Mar 27
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing has increased by £28.4m due to borrowing at lower interest rates to fund capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Earlier hospital discharge is creating sustained increase in homecare demand, a demand pressure outside the council's control
findings.detail: The paper identifies that people leaving hospital earlier in their recovery journey is fueling increased homecare demand. This is characterized as 'welcome' (policy-aligned) but 'impactful on services', indicating this is an expected ongoing shift rather than a temporary spike.
findings.matters: Demand drivers imposed by external policy (NHS discharge protocols) can create persistent budget pressure that the council cannot eliminate by efficiency alone. Understanding this is essential to assess whether the overspend will continue and requires structural budget change.
findings.figures: 1,100+ additional homecare hours per week; driven by earlier hospital discharge
findings.quote: The rise in this area for care support at home is also fuelled by people leaving hospital earlier in their recovery journey – which is welcome, but impactful on services.

findings.headline: Unachieved saving of £700k within Adult Commissioning Placements indicates budget assumptions not materializing
findings.detail: The paper reports an unachieved saving of £700k within Adult Commissioning Placements, but does not explicitly identify which saving target was missed or explain the reason. This suggests planned efficiencies or cost assumptions in the budget are not delivering as forecast.
findings.matters: Unachieved savings signal either overly optimistic budget assumptions or barriers to planned service efficiencies. This matters for assessing whether the overspend is temporary variance or a sign of structural issues with budget forecasting or service delivery.
findings.figures: £700k unachieved saving within Adult Commissioning Placements budget
findings.quote: There is still a reported overspend of £2,709k which also includes an unachieved saving of £700k.

findings.headline: Adult Commissioning Placements forecasting £863k overspend driven by increased homecare hours replacing residential care
findings.detail: Long-term residential and nursing placements have decreased (saving £499k) and short-term residential care has decreased (saving £521k), reflecting a deliberate policy shift toward supporting people living independently at home. However, homecare support has surged by over 1,100 commissioned hours per week, resulting in a net £863k overspend on this £76m budget line.
findings.matters: Adult services is the largest directorate budget item. This overspend shows that the shift from institutional to community-based care is creating budget pressure—unit costs or volume growth exceed the savings from placements closure. If this trend continues, it may require structural budget adjustment.
findings.figures: £863k overspend; £499k residential placement saving; £521k short-term care saving; 1,100+ homecare hours per week added since September 2025
findings.quote: The Adult Commissioning Placements budget forecasts an overspend of £863k... Homecare hours have increased significantly by over 1,100 commissioned hours per week since September 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Transformation programs expected to deliver multi-year returns while council cannot deliver baseline recurring savings, creating compounding budget risk
findings.detail: Blackpool's transformation programs are expected to deliver returns over 2026/27–2028/29, but their success is uncertain and benefits typically materialize slower than planned. The council is simultaneously failing to achieve its baseline recurring savings target. If transformation programs slip or deliver returns below forecast, the council has no buffer of achieved recurrent savings to absorb the slippage.
findings.matters: A council betting on transformation ROI while unable to hit baseline savings targets is doubly exposed to budget deterioration. Any program slippage or capital receipts shortfall could trigger a funding crisis within 12 months.
findings.figures: Transformation investment 2026/27: £4,966k; 2027/28: £5,065k; unresolved recurrent savings gap: £3,046k (combining unachievable and not-yet-found).
findings.quote: Work continues to deliver the original proposals as well as alternatives if they are unachievable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Council is using finite capital receipts (£11.2m deployed) to fund transformation programs instead of delivering recurrent savings—the £1.2m savings shortfall matches exactly the remaining capital receipts not yet deployed
findings.detail: Blackpool is using "Flexible Use of Capital Receipts" to finance transformation investments (Digital Transformation £1,127k; Early Help £2,358k; Ofsted improvement £183k; CQC improvement £566k; Adults Commissioning £429k; Financial Systems £243k). As at 30 June, £11,243k of £12,466k total planned capital receipts has been deployed, leaving £1,223k—which exactly matches the council's unachievable recurrent savings shortfall. This approach funds ongoing commitments from one-off asset sale proceeds that may not be repeated.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts to mask a recurring revenue budget deficit is not sustainable. If capital receipts dry up or asset sales slow, the council loses its funding source for transformation investments while the underlying revenue problem persists. This creates acute vulnerability.
findings.figures: Capital receipts deployment: £11,243k of £12,466k as at 30 June; transformation investments of £4,966k (2026/27) and £5,065k (2027/28); outstanding capital receipts of £1,223k exactly equals the unachievable recurrent savings gap.
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026 it is forecast that £11,243k of the £12.466m saving has been delivered. Work continues to deliver the original proposals as well as alternatives if they are unachievable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3p M3 2627 Directorate Budget Savings Performance
findings.headline: Only £1.4m of £7.5m recurrent savings achieved; £1.2m marked unachievable and £1.8m not yet found, with 100% of Children's Services target unachievable
findings.detail: As at 30 June 2026, Blackpool has achieved only £1,392k of its £7,500k savings target (18.6%). The council expects to deliver a further £4,885k by year-end, totalling £6,277k. However, £1,223k is explicitly marked "not able to be achieved" and £1,823k is "not yet found recurrently". Shortfalls are concentrated: Children's Services cannot achieve any of its £1,000k target (achieved £0k); Chief Executive cannot achieve £450k of £1,795k; Corporate cannot achieve £273k of £2,000k; Place has not identified £500k.
findings.matters: A council that cannot deliver planned savings must close the gap through borrowing, reserve drawdowns, or unplanned service reductions. The concentration of unachievable cuts in children's and corporate services suggests structural problems in those areas that will worsen over time.
findings.figures: £7,500k target; £1,392k achieved (18.6%); £4,885k forecast to achieve by year-end; £1,223k marked unachievable; £1,823k not found. Children's Services: 100% of £1,000k unachievable; Chief Executive: 25% of £1,795k unachievable.

findings.headline: Cumulative deficits of £10.3m and £2.2m projected by March 2027 in Growth and Prosperity
findings.detail: The paper projects cumulative deficits of £10,273k in Growth & Prosperity and £2,166k in Enterprise Zone by 31 March 2027. These cumulative positions show these service areas are consistently overspending, with deficits accumulating year-on-year rather than being recovered.
findings.matters: Cumulative deficits indicate structural rather than temporary problems. They represent a persistent drain on council reserves and suggest these services cannot pay for themselves from their budgets.
findings.figures: £10,273k Growth & Prosperity cumulative deficit; £2,166k Enterprise Zone cumulative deficit
findings.quote: It is expected that the Growth & Prosperity cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2027 will be £10,273k as it is assumed that the in -year deficit is covered by the Asset Disposal Plan and the Enterprise Zone cumulative deficit as at 31 March 2027 will be £2,166k.

findings.headline: £8.0m in-year overspend in Growth and Prosperity assumed to be covered by asset disposal
findings.detail: Growth and Prosperity is forecasting £8,049k overspend (£6,663k from schemes, £1,386k from Enterprise Zone). The paper states this in-year deficit is 'assumed' to be covered by the Asset Disposal Plan. Using one-time asset sales to fund a recurring operational deficit raises questions about sustainability if asset sales do not materialise as planned.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether a council's operational deficits are absorbed by reserves or funded by asset disposals. Asset sales are finite and non-recurring; they cannot sustainably fund recurring operational losses.
findings.figures: £8,049k overspend; £6,663k Growth & Prosperity schemes; £1,386k Enterprise Zone
findings.quote: The service is forecasting a £8,049k pressure which is made up of £6,663k from Growth & Prosperity schemes and £1,386k from the Enterprise Zone.

findings.headline: Debt refinancing was rejected because interest rates remain elevated with potential to rise further
findings.detail: The council considered refinancing its debt but rejected it because interest rates have not fallen as anticipated. The Bank of England's July 2026 guidance indicated rates could remain elevated or rise further due to geopolitical instability and energy costs.
findings.matters: Loss of refinancing as a debt management tool means the council is locked into higher financing costs with no opportunity to reduce the cost of capital.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: interest rates have not reduced to the extent anticipated. Furthermore, the Bank of England indicated in July that interest rates could remain elevated or potentially rise during 2026, reflecting ongoing inflationary pressures linked to geopolitical instability in the Middle East and rising energy costs.

findings.headline: The asset disposal programme is explicitly designed to mitigate the risk of requiring Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The council states that the Asset Disposal Programme is a critical enabling workstream that must be progressed proactively to reduce the likelihood of requiring EFS—a formal government intervention tool for councils in serious financial difficulty.
findings.matters: Mentioning EFS as a risk shows the council recognises itself as potentially vulnerable to government intervention for financial mismanagement; the disposal programme is framed as a mitigation strategy.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: The Asset Disposal Programme should be regarded as a critical enabling workstream and progressed proactively, as currently undertaken, to mitigate financial risk and reduce the likelihood of the Council requiring Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.headline: Capital financing costs (MRP and interest) now consume 7.3% of the council's total expenditure
findings.detail: The council's capital investment programme has driven increased borrowing and associated financing costs, which are now described as a significant element of both the revenue budget and the medium-term plan. These are irreducible costs committed for the life of the debt.
findings.matters: Capital financing costs crowd out discretionary spending and reduce budget flexibility; they are fixed commitments that cannot be cut without breaching loan covenants.
findings.figures: approximately 7.3% of total expenditure
findings.quote: Capital financing costs now represent a significant element within both the Revenue Budget and the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP), accounting for approximately 7.3% of total expenditure.

findings.headline: Asset disposals are required to fill the budget gap in 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The council explicitly relies on sales of non-operational assets to meet budget deficits in two consecutive years. The programme targets circa £30m in receipts by the end of 2027/28 and these receipts are budgeted to support financial sustainability and maintain reserves.
findings.matters: One-off asset sales to balance the revenue budget signal structural budget problems and are not a sustainable long-term funding source.
findings.figures: circa £30m by the end of the 2027/28 financial year
findings.quote: The Council's 2026/27 budget and Medium-Term Financial Plan recognises the need for effective use of financial receipts in the medium term through the use of disposal of non-operational assets, to meet the Council's budget gap for 2026/27 and 2027/28

findings.headline: Beach Patrol forecasts a £70k seasonal cost pressure
findings.detail: Commercial Services reports a £70k forecast overspend specifically attributed to seasonal beach patrol costs.
findings.matters: Recurring seasonal cost pressures indicate whether base budgets adequately absorb predictable variations in service demand.
findings.quote: There is a pressure of £70k forecast in Beach Patrol due to the cost of seasonal patrols.

findings.headline: Parking Services forecasts an £868k income shortfall despite patronage being slightly up
findings.detail: The council budgeted £4,342k parking income but is now forecasting only £3,474k, a shortfall of £868k. Unusually, the paper states that patronage is currently slightly up on the same time last year, making the income decline unexplained.
findings.matters: Parking income is a material discretionary revenue source for councils. An unexplained income shortfall despite rising patronage signals potential issues with pricing, enforcement, or customer mix that warrant investigation and could impact budget delivery.
findings.figures: Budget £4,342k, forecast £3,474k, variance £868k overspend
findings.quote: Parking Services is expecting a pressure in 2026/27 of £868k which reflects the income and patronage to date which is currently slightly up on the same time last year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3f M3 2627 Strategic Leisure Assets Directorate
findings.headline: Previous 2034/35 break-even plan being replaced; new medium-term plan not yet published following governance restructure
findings.detail: A new medium-term financial plan is being worked up following the creation of Blackpool Tourism Limited and changes to management arrangements. The previous MTFP expected cumulative break-even by 2034/35, but this trajectory is being abandoned before the new plan is issued.
findings.matters: The replacement of a long-term plan partway through its forecast period suggests the previous assumptions were not being met. Until the new plan is published, there is uncertainty about whether the governance restructure will address the structural deficit or merely manage it differently.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3f M3 2627 Strategic Leisure Assets Directorate
findings.headline: Strategic Leisure Assets running sustained annual deficit of £1,721k, cumulative deficit now £12,474k
findings.detail: The service forecasts a £1.7m overspend for 2026/27, which will be transferred to an earmarked reserve as per the original 2011 Executive decision. The cumulative deficit has now reached £12,474k. These are historic assets (Blackpool Tower and Winter Gardens) that were chronically under-invested by previous private owners, and the reserve is specifically earmarked for their future investment and maintenance.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how quickly the council's reserves are depleting and whether reserves earmarked for specific assets are adequate. An annual deficit of £1.7m accumulated over time raises questions about the long-term sustainability of this position and whether the reserve will be sufficient for capital investment in aging assets.
findings.figures: £1,721k forecast overspend 2026/27; £12,474k cumulative deficit by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Strategic Leisure Assets, which largely relates to the investment in key historic and economic assets of Blackpool Tower and the Winter Gardens, forecast a pressure of £1,721k.

findings.headline: Treasury Management forecasting £772k overspend due to interest rate pressures not materializing as budgeted
findings.detail: The council budgeted Treasury Management on the assumption of Bank of England rate reductions in line with economic predictions. The Iran conflict and subsequent oil price impacts reversed this position, creating an unbudgeted interest cost pressure. The council states this pressure will only reduce if interest rates themselves fall.
findings.matters: Interest rate cost overruns reduce financial headroom directly and indicate the council's debt servicing assumptions were optimistic; a lender would need to understand whether this is a one-off timing issue or a structural cost
findings.figures: Treasury Management: adjusted cash limited budget £26,837k, forecast outturn £29,289k, variance £772k overspend. Corporate Services total forecast overspend £772k for year to March 2027.
findings.quote: Treasury Management is forecasting a cost pressure of £7 72k linked to interest rates. The budget anticipated a small amount of Bank of England rate reductions, in line with most economic predictions, unfortunately the conflict in Iran and the associated impact on oil prices and the worldwide economy have reversed this position.

findings.headline: Other Supported Housing income 23% short at £224k, while mainstream housing tracks plan
findings.detail: Other Supported Housing is projected at £224k against £290k budgeted (£66k shortfall), while Resilience Housing (£1,154k) and Emergency Housing (£1,182k) are both hitting budget exactly. The divergence in the supported housing line suggests either occupancy change or rent mix variation.
findings.matters: Supported housing income variations can signal occupancy constraints or rent-setting challenges in high-needs provision; divergence from budget on this line alone warrants investigation into whether capacity or demand has shifted.
findings.figures: Other Supported Housing £224k projected vs £290k budget (variance £66k, 23%).

findings.headline: Working balances projected to finish at £2,318k, £317k below the budgeted £2,635k
findings.detail: The variance comprises a £168k lower opening balance and a £149k shortfall in the contribution from operations. Opening balances started at £1,363k against a budget of £1,531k. Despite expenditure coming in £61k better than budget, total income fell £210k short, constraining the year's surplus contribution to just £955k against £1,104k budgeted.
findings.matters: For a lender, HRA reserve trends matter to overall council sustainability; a 12% reduction from plan raises questions about whether the opening position reflects carried-forward 2025/26 issues or whether current operational performance is materially weaker than budgeted.
findings.figures: Opening balance £1,363k (budget £1,531k, variance £168k). Full-year contribution projected £955k (budget £1,104k, variance £149k). Closing balance projected £2,318k (budget £2,635k, variance £317k).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3h M3 2627 Community and Environmental Services
findings.headline: Waste disposal cost pressures from rising gate fees and volumes are being managed through the waste reserve
findings.detail: The paper notes that waste services face challenges due to increasing waste disposal costs from rising gate fees and increased waste volumes. The council states these pressures are expected to be met through the waste reserve, indicating the reserve is being drawn down to absorb market-driven cost volatility.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing operational cost pressures (not exceptional items) suggests either that budget assumptions are under-set or that external market pressures are creating structural cost mismatches that may recur.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: There are challenges within the service due to increasing waste disposal costs as a result of increased waste volumes arising and gate fees. Any pressures within waste disposal are expected to be met through the waste reserve.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3h M3 2627 Community and Environmental Services
findings.headline: Blackpool's £776k new food waste collection service is dependent on EPR grant funding that has not yet been confirmed
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £776k cost for the new statutory food waste collection service. This cost is entirely expected to be funded by Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Grant funding, which has not been confirmed to arrive in the year. If the grant is delayed or does not materialise, this creates an unfunded £776k pressure.
findings.matters: Core statutory service costs should not depend on external grant flows the council cannot control. A lender needs to know whether the council has identified a fallback if this grant doesn't arrive.
findings.quote: There is also a pressure in relation to the new Food Waste collection service, which is forecast to cost £776k. This is expected to be funded through Extended Producer responsibility (EPR) Grant funding to be received in the year.

findings.headline: Children's Services Directorate forecasts total overspend of £4.203m for 2026/27
findings.detail: The combined £4.2m overspend across the directorate requires funding from elsewhere in the council. The largest driver is the £3.4m children's social care placements pressure, plus £819k from education transport.
findings.matters: A material directorate-wide overspend indicates the council's budget assumptions are not holding. For a lender, this signals either reserve drawdown or the need for within-year reallocation, both of which weaken the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £4,203k directorate overspend; £3,384k from placements; £819k from education
findings.quote: As at the end of June 2026 the Children's Services Directorate is forecasting an overspend of £4,203k for the financial year to March 2027.

findings.headline: Education transport overspend of £819k driven by growing EHCP numbers and cost pressures
findings.detail: The Children's Transport Service faces demand-led cost growth linked to the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans. This appears to be a structural service pressure.
findings.matters: EHCP numbers are a leading indicator of high-cost intervention demand. Rising transport costs for this cohort signal ongoing structural pressures that are unlikely to ease without policy change.
findings.figures: £819k overspend
findings.quote: Education is expected to be £819k overspent, mainly relating to Children's Transport Service due to demand pressures linked to Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) numbers and increased costs associated with the service.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placements forecast £3.384m overspend from new entries exceeding exits
findings.detail: The service is experiencing more children entering care than leaving, creating placement cost pressures. Residential placements are forecast to reduce from 78 to 64 by year-end, but per-placement costs remain elevated. Current LAC numbers stand at 531 children (188 per 10,000 of 0-17 year olds).
findings.matters: This is the single largest budget pressure in a demand-led service. A lender needs to understand how a council will fund a £3.4m gap and whether reserves are adequate to absorb it, particularly given Blackpool's prior financial difficulties.
findings.figures: £3,384k overspend; 531 children in care; 78 residential placements at 30 June 2026; forecast 64 by 31 March 2027; 188 per 10,000 of 0-17 year olds
findings.quote: Children's Social Care Placements are fo recasting an overspend of £3,384k, mainly due to new -to-care placements being higher than those exiting care and the additional support required following the breakdown of high-cost placements.

findings.headline: Visit Blackpool forecasting £350k revenue shortfall due to Tower lifts operational failures
findings.detail: Visit Blackpool, transferred to this directorate, is forecasting a £350k budget pressure. The service depends on achieving £1.5m in additional income from commercial operations (Sandcastle and Winter Gardens), but operational problems with the Tower lifts are reducing visitor numbers and revenue. Management is preparing an investment case to replace the lifts to recover lost income.
findings.matters: The council is relying on commercial operation income to balance its budget, but capital asset failures are eroding that income. This signals both a £350k near-term shortfall and upcoming capital investment needs for asset replacement.
findings.figures: £350k pressure; £1.5m increased income target; Tower lifts operational issues
findings.quote: This service is forecasting a £ 350k pressure. This takes into account the target of £1.5m increased income from Blackpool's commercial operations. Blackpool Tourism Limited (BTL) has delivered strong results so far relating to the Sandcastle and Winter Gardens, though some of this has been offset by potential income lost due to operational issues with the Tower lifts.

findings.headline: Council is using reserves to balance the 2026/27 revenue budget
findings.detail: Net cost of services is forecast at £227,822k against a budget of £221,327k (£6,495k overspend). After reserve contributions and transfers, the council will take £5,145k from general balances to reach a balanced account. This is the second consecutive year of drawing reserves to fund revenue.
findings.matters: Councils that balance revenue by drawing reserves rather than finding permanent savings or reductions face declining financial stability and eventual insolvency risk.
findings.figures: Net cost variance £6,495k; total drawdown from balances £5,145k; total net expenditure to be met from public funds £227,875k
findings.quote: ADDED TO/(TAKEN FROM) BALANCES 6,900 6,900 (5,145) 1,755 (5,145)

findings.headline: Children's Services forecasts a £4,203k overspend against a £82,602k budget
findings.detail: Children's services is projected to spend £86,805k against a budget of £82,602k — a 5.1% variance. This is one of the largest single-service overspends and suggests significant cost or demand pressures in a statutory function.
findings.matters: Unexplained demand-driven overspends in children's services, a statutory obligation, signal underlying cost drivers that will recur and cannot be easily controlled.
findings.figures: Budget £82,602k, forecast spend £86,805k, variance £4,203k

findings.headline: General working balances will fall to £2,080k (0.9% of budget) by March 2027
findings.detail: Opening balance April 2026 was £325k (0.14% of budget). The council will draw £5,145k from reserves to fund the year's overspends, leaving just £2,080k unearmarked. Minimum guidance is typically 2–3% of budget; the council will fall critically short.
findings.matters: Critically depleted reserves prevent the council from absorbing any unexpected shock and indicate the underlying budget is structurally unsustainable without reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Opening £325k, forecast drawdown £5,145k, closing £2,080k; net budget ~£230m
